children.text: Key Takeaways
Auto insurance usually follows the vehicle, so the owner’s policy typically pays first.
The vehicle owner may still face financial responsibility when a permitted driver causes a crash.
The at-fault driver’s insurance usually pays when another driver causes the accident.
Insurance coverage may change if the driver used the vehicle without permission.
After a crash, seek medical care, report the accident, and document evidence.
No one expects to get a call saying their car was just in an accident, especially when someone else was behind the wheel. When that happens, a lot of questions come up quickly.
Who’s responsible?
Whose insurance pays? And most importantly, what happens if someone else is driving my car and gets in an accident, or “
What happens if someone else crashes your car?”
and who is ultimately responsible for the damages.
In Colorado, when a driver borrows your car with your clear permission and is involved in an accident, your insurance usually applies first to cover the damage. This is because, as stated by the
Colorado DMV

, insurance typically follows the car, not the person behind the wheel. Still, every situation is unique, and both the circumstances of the crash and the fine print in your policy can affect who is responsible and what’s covered. That’s why the
car accident lawyers
at

work with drivers across Denver to help them understand their rights and responsibilities in these stressful situations.
Understanding Car Insurance Coverage
In many situations, the answer depends on how
auto insurance coverage

is structured. Most auto policies are tied to the vehicle itself, which means the insurance attached to the car usually provides the first layer of protection when an accident causes property damage or injuries. When the vehicle owner gives someone permission to drive the car, insurers typically treat that situation as permissive use, allowing the owner’s liability coverage to apply to the crash.
Coverage can still depend on the details of the policy, since liability limits, exclusions, and other conditions determine how much protection is available if damages exceed the policy’s limits.

children.text: Am I Liable If Someone Else Drove My Car and Caused an Accident?

Yes, the vehicle owner can sometimes be financially responsible after a crash when another person was driving the car, mainly because the insurance policy attached to the vehicle often applies first. When a driver has permission to use the car and causes an accident, the owner’s liability coverage typically becomes the primary source of payment for property damage or injury claims. This does not necessarily mean the owner personally caused the crash, but it does mean the insurance tied to the vehicle may be used to resolve the claim.
Complications can arise when damages exceed policy limits, since the driver’s own insurance may then provide additional coverage depending on the circumstances.
Who Pays When Someone Else Crashes Your Car?

The vehicle owner’s insurance policy usually pays first when another driver causes a crash while using the car with permission. Because auto insurance generally follows the vehicle, that policy often serves as the primary source of funds for injury claims and property damage. The outcome still depends on fault, policy limits, and whether other insurance coverage is available.
When evaluating
“What happens if someone else crashes your car?”
, payment responsibility often follows these patterns:
Owner’s policy:
The vehicle owner’s liability insurance usually serves as the primary coverage when the driver has permission to use the car.
Driver’s insurance:
The driver’s personal auto policy may provide secondary coverage if damages exceed the owner’s policy limits.
At-fault third party:
Another driver’s insurer may ultimately pay when that driver caused the crash.
These factors help determine which insurance policy becomes responsible for covering the resulting losses.
What Happens If the Accident Wasn’t Their Fault?

When the driver of your car did not cause the accident, the insurance company for the driver who caused the crash is usually responsible for paying the damages. Liability generally follows the party whose negligence caused the collision, meaning their insurer may cover vehicle repairs, medical expenses, and other losses related to the crash.
Insurance companies often review police reports
, witness statements, and other evidence before determining which driver is legally responsible.
Situations like this often arise when someone asks,
“What happens if someone else crashes your car?”
, since the final outcome can depend on proving that another driver’s actions caused the accident.
Exceptions and Considerations
When someone else is driving your vehicle and is involved in a crash, several legal and insurance-related concerns may arise.
Negligent Entrustment

You may be considered legally responsible if you knowingly lent your vehicle to a driver who posed a clear risk, such as someone with a known record of drunk driving or repeated reckless behavior. This scenario falls under a legal concept called negligent entrustment.
Vicarious Liability
In situations where the other driver was using your vehicle to run errands for you or acting in your interest, you could still be held legally responsible under what’s known as vicarious liability.
Policy Exclusions

Insurance policies can contain clauses that limit or exclude coverage for specific people or uses. That’s why reviewing your policy carefully and understanding any restrictions before letting someone else drive your car is important.
Uninsured/Underinsured Motorist Coverage

If the at-fault driver is uninsured or lacks sufficient coverage, your UM/UIM (uninsured/underinsured motorist) coverage may help cover expenses that exceed what their insurance can pay. This protection is especially important when damage or injuries go beyond the limits of the driver’s own policy.
What Happens If Someone Takes Your Car Without Permission and Causes an Accident?

When someone drives your car without your knowledge or approval and crashes it, your insurance provider may refuse to pay for the damages. Even though insurance typically follows the vehicle, it often requires that the driver have authorized use.
Here’s what may happen:
Coverage may be denied if the insurance company determines the driver didn’t have permission. The driver’s own auto policy, if they have one, might then be responsible.
Your uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage may apply if the unauthorized driver doesn’t have insurance.
Liability might shift to the driver’s personal insurance if they had no permission to operate your car. If they’re uninsured, your UM/UIM coverage may become the next source of financial protection.
Negligent entrustment can still apply if you knowingly allowed an unsafe driver to take the car, even informally.
Insurance providers will investigate thoroughly, evaluating permission, exclusions, and liability shifts.
Filing a police report is essential to prove a lack of permission and help support your insurance position.
You may need legal action if the unauthorized driver lacks insurance and the damages exceed your coverage.
Criminal charges may apply, as taking a vehicle without permission can be prosecuted as motor vehicle theft in Colorado.
A common concern we hear from clients is,
“What happens if someone else crashes your car?”

especially when there’s damage that exceeds policy limits. In these cases, any financial responsibility beyond coverage might fall on the driver, or in some situations, on you. It all depends on the fault and whether your insurer chooses to defend or settle.
Steps to Take Immediately After an Accident

After a crash involving your vehicle, acting quickly can protect your health and help prevent complications with insurance claims. Colorado law also requires drivers involved in a collision to stop and remain at the scene until certain responsibilities are fulfilled. According to the
Colorado Revised Statutes § 42-4-1602
, drivers involved in a crash must stop at or near the scene and remain there long enough to exchange required information and comply with reporting duties.

Taking a few key actions immediately after the accident can help protect your rights and support any insurance or legal claim that may follow. The following steps explain what drivers should prioritize after a crash.
Seek Medical Attention

Seeking medical attention as soon as possible after a crash helps protect both your health and any future insurance claim. Some injuries, including concussions, soft tissue damage, and internal trauma, may not show symptoms immediately after an accident. A prompt medical evaluation allows doctors to identify hidden injuries and begin treatment before complications develop.

Early treatment also creates medical records that document when symptoms appeared and how injuries were diagnosed. These records often become important evidence in insurance claims or legal disputes. Waiting too long to seek care can make it harder to link injuries to the crash and may complicate efforts to recover compensation.
Contacting Your Insurance Company

Notifying your insurance company soon after an accident helps begin the claims process and ensures the incident is documented while details remain fresh. Most insurance policies require prompt reporting, even when another person was driving your vehicle at the time of the crash. Early notice allows the insurer to review the circumstances and determine how coverage may apply.
When reporting the accident, insurers usually request several key details:
Accident information:
The date, location, and basic description of how the crash occurred.
Driver details:
The name and contact information of the person operating your vehicle.
Supporting evidence:
Photos, witness information, and any available police reports.
Providing clear and accurate information helps insurers evaluate the claim more efficiently.
Gathering Evidence and Filing a Police Report
Collecting accurate information after a crash

helps establish what happened and supports insurance or legal claims that may follow. Evidence gathered at the scene often becomes important when insurers review the incident or when liability is disputed. Photographs, witness details, and official reports can all help clarify how the collision occurred.
Several forms of documentation can strengthen the record of the accident:
Scene photographs:
Images of vehicle damage, road conditions, and traffic signs help document the crash.
Witness information:
Names and contact details allow investigators to verify what others saw.
Police report:
Officers who respond to the crash usually collect key information needed for official records.
According to the
Colorado Division of Motor Vehicles crash records guidance

, when an officer investigates the accident and gathers the necessary details, drivers generally do not need to submit additional crash forms unless the Department of Revenue later sends instructions.

An attorney can review the circumstances of the accident, communicate with insurers, and guide you through the claims process.
